title: US Consumers Still Pay Less for Power Than Europe Despite Price-Hike Headlines | BloombergNEF
gist: BloombergNEF finds US households paid $173/MWh for power in 2025 versus $435 in Germany, $391 in the UK and $333 in Australia, with US real residential prices up only 3% in 2019-2025. European industry also pays far more ($226-327/MWh vs $110 US and $89 China), a competitiveness handicap for electrified sectors such as aluminum and steel.

insights.claim: Average retail power prices for households and industry rose faster than inflation over 2019-2025 in about three-quarters of the 37 markets in BNEF's report, with industry up 24% in real terms versus 12% for households.
insights.speaker: Victoria Cuming
insights.so_what: Industrial electricity costs are inflating faster than household ones, squeezing competitiveness.
insights.quote: Industry saw a bigger average increase, of 24% in real terms compared with 12% for households.
insights.locator: Many consumers pay more for power today

insights.claim: Markets insulated by domestic energy resources including renewables, plus regulation and price-stabilisation measures, such as Canada, Brazil and New Zealand, kept 2025 tariffs near 2019 levels in real terms.
insights.speaker: Victoria Cuming
insights.so_what: Domestic resource endowment and regulatory buffers are the main protection against price shocks.
insights.locator: Other markets have experienced less volatility

insights.claim: Deregulated US markets like California and New Jersey, plus South Korea and Spain, saw markedly higher prices driven by rising network and subsidy costs and the end of price-stabilisation measures.
insights.speaker: Victoria Cuming
insights.so_what: Network and subsidy cost pass-through, not just fuel, is lifting retail tariffs in some markets.
insights.locator: However, prices were markedly higher in deregulated US markets

insights.claim: China, India, Mexico and Russia saw falling real residential tariffs and some of the lowest retail rates, reflecting heavy regulatory intervention, subsidies and domestic energy resources.
insights.speaker: Victoria Cuming
insights.so_what: State-managed pricing gives these economies a power-cost edge for electrification and industry.
insights.locator: China, India, Mexico and Russia bucked the trend

insights.claim: The 2021-23 energy crisis sparked by Russia's invasion of Ukraine drove much of the volatility, hitting gas-importing markets hardest, and recent retail price rises have also been linked to the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Victoria Cuming
insights.so_what: Gas-import dependence remains the key vulnerability of retail power prices to geopolitical shocks.
insights.locator: Since 2019, markets like the UK, Japan and Argentina

themes.theme: US vs Europe and Australia residential prices

insights.claim: US average real residential power prices rose 3% in 2019-2025 across the 50 states and DC, and 20 states saw decreases, even though electricity rates are rising up the political agenda ahead of the November midterms.
insights.speaker: Victoria Cuming
insights.so_what: Headline price-hike narratives overstate the average US household burden, but remain a political risk.
insights.quote: Electricity rates are fast climbing the US political agenda, especially as the November midterm elections approach.
insights.locator: Residential power prices have risen slightly in the US

insights.claim: In 2025 US households paid an average $173/MWh versus $435/MWh in Germany, $391/MWh in the UK and $333/MWh in Australia.
insights.speaker: Victoria Cuming
insights.so_what: US consumers hold a large price advantage over major peers, supporting electrification economics.
insights.quote: On average, US households pay less than other major economies, at $173 per megawatt-hour in 2025
insights.locator: Residential power prices have risen slightly in the US

insights.claim: Europe's higher household prices stem partly from using consumer bills to fund green, social and public support, whereas the US and others often fund these via the general budget; European bills also carry higher network and sometimes wholesale and supply costs.
insights.speaker: Victoria Cuming
insights.so_what: Shifting policy costs from bills to budgets is a lever for lowering European retail prices.
insights.locator: Europe's higher prices are partly due to higher policy costs

insights.claim: Australia had the largest rise in household power prices in the report, 186% in real terms over 2019-2025, driven first by high fossil fuel prices and supply constraints and later by generator outages, high demand periods and rising network costs.
insights.speaker: Victoria Cuming
insights.so_what: Australia is the outlier case of price surge, giving it among the highest retail rates covered.
insights.locator: Australia had the biggest rise in household prices

insights.claim: Residential consumers pay more per unit than industry in most markets studied because households bear higher network and customer-service costs, while large industrial users spread fixed costs, negotiate harder and sometimes get preferential tax or policy treatment.
insights.speaker: Victoria Cuming
insights.so_what: Industrial tariff design, not just generation cost, determines energy-intensive competitiveness.
insights.locator: Residential consumers pay higher electricity rates than industry

insights.claim: Power prices can make or break industries like aluminum, which is heavily electrified, and steel, where electrification is a key decarbonisation route.
insights.speaker: Victoria Cuming
insights.so_what: Expensive power threatens both competitiveness and decarbonisation of heavy industry in high-price regions.
insights.locator: Yet power prices can still make or break many industrial sectors

insights.claim: In 2025 industrial power averaged $327/MWh in the UK and $226/MWh in Germany versus $110/MWh in the US and $89/MWh in China, leaving European industry at a competitive disadvantage despite policy efforts to limit rates.
insights.speaker: Victoria Cuming
insights.so_what: Europe's industrial power gap to the US and China is roughly 2-4x, a structural headwind to reshoring and heavy industry.

insights.claim: High retail prices can undermine market competitiveness and delay electrification, which could improve energy security, making them a policy trigger beyond household pocketbooks.
insights.speaker: Victoria Cuming
insights.so_what: Price-cap and relief pressure may push policymakers to intervene in power markets.
insights.locator: Retail electricity rates can hit pocketbooks hard
